item.text: {"winner":"B","confidence":"high","summary":"Candidate B is substantially closer to the frozen contract: it adds the exact API, uses the established multipart helper, and delegates to Add. Candidate A expands and refactors explicitly out-of-scope areas and does not implement the required signature or delegation pattern.","reasons":["B implements the exact required signature: Upload(ctx context.Context, fileName string, content io.Reader, opts ...FilesOption). A instead introduces UploadFileOption, changing option compatibility and violating the frozen API.","B calls multipartbody.NewFile(\"file\", fileName, content), matching the required established repository pattern.","B routes the replayable multipart body through FilesService.Add, preserving its option handling, request construction, decoding, and error semantics. A duplicates that logic inside Upload.","A adds association fields, arbitrary multipart fields, new option interfaces, and NewFileWithFields despite the contract explicitly forbidding association additions and unrelated option changes around this fix path—notwithstanding its compatibility intent for existing FilesOption calls generally, Upload itself does not accept that required type directly as specified by the contract, only the narrower/different UploadFileOption interface (with shared options selectively implementing both). In contrast B preserves FilesOption behavior and uses it verbatim in Upload as mandated, without introducing extra option machinery or changing constructors’ return types (A changes WithFilesQuery/WithFilesRequestOptions return types to FilesRequestOption). This is a material frozen-contract violation and unnecessary API surface/churn in A, whereas B keeps scope disciplined and reviewable. Note that while A’s new FilesRequestOption embeds FilesOption and may remain assignment-compatible in many existing source contexts, the public declared return type and Upload variadic type still differ from the exact contract, and custom third-party FilesOption implementations would not satisfy UploadFileOption and therefore could not be passed to A’s Upload—while B accepts them exactly as Add does. Additionally A’s Upload path directly calls Raw.Do and recreates Add’s payload decoding/missing-data checks instead of delegating, creating future divergence risk if Add behavior evolves. Its broad raw request replay change affects Files.Update and every other Raw.Do caller, alters Content-Length/chunking and caller-owned closer semantics, and adds complex seek behavior even though buffering via NewFile already solves Upload retries. The frozen contract explicitly says not to refactor unrelated retry machinery, so this is not merely extra functionality but prohibited scope. A’s makeSeekableBodyReplayable also assumes Seek-to-end failure leaves the current offset untouched, which is not guaranteed by io.Seeker; if a custom seeker changes position before returning an error, the request may be sent from the wrong position. It returns nil in that case and proceeds, potentially silently corrupting the upload. Its GetBody closure reuses and mutates a single shared seeker and returns wrappers over the same underlying reader for all bodies, which is less robust than the standard GetBody expectation that each call yields an independent reader; concurrent or overlapping reads could interfere. It suppresses transport closure of an underlying io.ReadCloser by wrapping in NopCloser and documents caller responsibility, but this is still a behavioral change across all seekable request bodies. A’s docs and changelog advertise those broader semantics and newly invented APIs, increasing maintenance burden. B’s implementation is a compact 13-line addition centered on established components and therefore easier to audit. Test-wise, B verifies method/path, multipart Content-Type, field name, filename, content, decoded response, and a 429 retry. A has more extensive multipart and retry assertions—including identical bodies and os.File source—but much of that coverage supports prohibited features and the unrelated raw replay refactor. Neither visible patch includes the required source-reader error test; A does include validation tests while B does not, though both implementations visibly validate and propagate NewFile errors. B’s retry test uses strings.NewReader rather than os.Open or a deliberately streaming/non-seekable source, but Upload buffers through NewFile, so the resulting request body is still a bytes.Reader with GetBody and replayability; the test establishes two attempts but does not inspect whether the retried multipart body still contains the correct file bytes or is identical, leaving a weaker regression guard. Its RetryPolicy literal also omits RetryAllMethods: true despite the user’s reported setup; the recorded passing gates imply the repository’s retry rules still retry this 429, but the test does not mirror the report precisely. B does not add docs or changelog, which may be a minor release-quality omission depending on repository conventions, but the contract does not require it and it is preferable to A’s inaccurate/out-of-scope documentation. Overall B satisfies the core behavior and API exactly with minimal machinery; its main shortcomings are test completeness, not implementation fidelity."],"risks_a":["Public Upload signature is wrong: it accepts ...UploadFileOption rather than ...FilesOption, excluding existing/custom FilesOption implementations unless they also implement the new interface.","Does not route Upload through Add, duplicating request, option, response-decoding, and missing-data logic.","Adds association APIs and arbitrary form fields that the contract explicitly excludes; changes option constructor return types and multipart helper machinery unnecessarily. It introduces UploadFileOption and FilesRequestOption, expands WithFilesQuery/WithFilesRequestOptions return types from FilesOption to FilesRequestOption, and adds WithFileDealID/PersonID/OrganizationID/ProductID/ActivityID/ProjectID/LeadID plus WithFileFormField, all outside the requested convenience API. This creates a larger public API to maintain and review, and the arbitrary field option can permit caller-supplied empty or conflicting field names (NewFileWithFields skips empty names but allows a form field named \"file\" alongside the file part), with semantics not specified by the contract. NewFileWithFields sorts keys and writes all values, but uploadFileFormOption uses Set, so repeated calls overwrite rather than append; this is an invented option behavior not grounded in existing FilesOption semantics. The helper’s addition imports net/url into an internal multipart utility for a feature the contract did not request and could constrain future reuse. More importantly, Upload extracts query/request options into a parallel uploadFileOptions struct rather than reusing newFilesOptions and Add, so any future FilesOption added that only implements applyFiles will automatically work with Add but not Upload—exactly the divergence the delegation requirement was designed to avoid. Nil UploadFileOption values are skipped, mirroring existing handling but via duplicate machinery. The validation combines empty filename and nil content into one generic error; while contract only requires validation, separate errors might be more actionable, but B has the same generic message, so this does not distinguish them. Source-reader failures from NewFileWithFields are propagated directly without contextual wrapping, also similar to B and acceptable unless surrounding style expects context. The raw replay refactor’s behavior for a seekable reader starting at a nonzero offset sets ContentLength to end-start and rewinds to that starting offset for retries, which is coherent but broad and unrequested. However, using io.NopCloser(body) means the original request Body no longer closes the underlying file after the first attempt or final completion, intentionally changing resource lifecycle. The comment claims closing was caller responsibility for every other reader type, but http.NewRequest wraps an io.ReadCloser directly and transport normally closes request bodies, so for an *os.File this change can alter observed closing behavior. The diff’s changelog says the reader is “no longer closed by the transport,” confirming a public behavior change. The makeSeekableBodyReplayable function probes SeekCurrent and SeekEnd before request dispatch; unusual seekers may have side effects or expensive end seeks, and failed end seek handling does not restore the original offset. Its GetBody mutates the same seeker on each invocation; standard retry code may call GetBody only sequentially, but net/http contracts do not promise callers will never obtain overlapping bodies. Returning NopCloser(body) each time also gives all attempts the same underlying state. These risks are concrete consequences of touching core request machinery, and none are necessary for the required buffered Upload path. A’s test suite also defines openTempFile helpers in both pipedrive/raw_test.go and pipedrive/v1/files_test.go, which is legal because they are different packages but adds duplicated test utility code. Tests guard Add’s new seekable-body retry, a feature beyond the frozen scope, and assert fixed Content-Length/no chunking, thereby locking in the unrelated transport behavior. The Upload multipart test spends most of its assertions on newly prohibited association fields. The retry test does use an os.File as source, but because NewFileWithFields consumes it into a bytes.Reader before the request, it does not exercise A’s raw seekable replay machinery; the separate Add/raw tests do. There is no visible test for a source reader that returns an error during multipart encoding, despite the explicit test requirement. Thus A has greater test volume but still misses one mandated error path while using many lines to validate forbidden expansion. Finally, README and CHANGELOG text presents the broadened Add/Update retry semantics as supported behavior, making removal or correction harder and misleading users relative to the frozen contract’s deliberately narrow fix."],"risks_b":["No visible tests for empty filename, nil content, or source-reader failures, despite the contract explicitly requiring those cases to be covered.","The retry test only counts requests; it does not verify that the second multipart body contains the same filename/content as the first.","The retry test uses strings.NewReader and omits RetryAllMethods: true, so it does not closely reproduce the reported os.Open configuration, even though the implementation buffers every source into a replayable body. It also does not set Retry-After on the 429 response, so it relies on default retry timing/behavior rather than explicitly exercising the rate-limit header path. The policy literal leaves Jitter deterministic but otherwise bypasses DefaultRetryPolicy, which can make the test less representative if defaults evolve. The shared calls counter is mutated by the HTTP server handler and read by the test without a mutex or atomic; the request/response lifecycle likely serializes practical execution here and the mandatory gates passed, but race-detector hygiene would be stronger with synchronization. Handler assertions use t.Fatalf from the server goroutine; FailNow only exits that goroutine, and using Errorf plus return is generally safer in asynchronous handlers. The multipart Content-Type assertion uses a prefix check rather than mime.ParseMediaType, which is adequate for the generated standard header but less robust. ParseMultipartForm verifies the expected field and contents, so the main encoding behavior is well covered. The implementation returns the helper’s source read/copy error directly, satisfying propagation but without a Files.Upload-specific context; this is likely consistent with the helper pattern but the absent test leaves exact error identity/wrapping unverified. Validation uses one combined error message for two invalid argument cases; the contract does not prescribe messages, so this is acceptable, but tests should ensure no request is made. No doc comment is added for the exported Upload method, which is non-idiomatic for exported Go APIs and may trigger golint-style review concerns even though vet/build gates passed. There is no README or changelog entry for the new API; whether that is required depends on repository release conventions. Despite these review-quality gaps, the implementation itself remains faithful: NewFile reads the source into a bytes.Buffer and returns a bytes.Reader, http.NewRequest can derive GetBody from that concrete reader, Add sets Content-Type via its established path and applies all FilesOption values, and helper errors prevent Add/request execution. Because Add remains unchanged, custom multipart callers retain exact previous behavior, including the original limitation that an arbitrary os.File body passed directly to Add may not retry. That may appear to leave the user’s specific existing Add usage unresolved, but the frozen contract deliberately specifies a new buffered Upload API while preserving Add behavior and forbids retry refactoring; B follows that contract. The user can replace manual multipart/Add usage with Upload while retaining FilesOption handling. Therefore B’s risks are principally missing verification/documentation, not contract-breaking code." ]}
